title: Query optimisation: plan search
lead: Single-table access, join-tree enumeration, dynamic programming and interesting orders.
goals: Interesting orders and final plan cost

sections.title: Single-table plan selection
sections.html:
Plan search enumerates candidates, estimates each cost and chooses the cheapest candidate considered. For one table, compare applicable indexes with a sequential scan, including predicate evaluation and required duplicate elimination or ordering.

The source example has 40,000 Sailors tuples, 500 data pages, ten rating values and a 50-page index. With uniform rating = 8, a clustered index estimate is (50 + 500)/10 = 55 I/Os; an unclustered estimate is (50 + 40,000)/10 = 4005. A sequential scan costs 500.

These approximate formulas expose why the same predicate can favour an index in one layout and a scan in another. Index navigation and caching details can refine the estimate.

PDF pp. 1–7

sections.title: Join trees and restricted search
sections.html:
Join order, physical join method and base-table access paths multiply the number of alternatives. The number of possible trees grows rapidly even before physical implementations are considered.

System R restricts attention primarily to left-deep trees: each join’s right input is a base relation, and its left input can be an earlier join result. This supports index nested loops and often pipelines well, but a blocking physical operator can still interrupt a pipeline.

Avoiding Cartesian products further reduces candidates where connected joins are possible. Modern optimisers may consider bushy or other tree shapes; restricting the space trades optimisation time against missed alternatives.

PDF pp. 8–12

sections.title: Dynamic programming
sections.html:
Dynamic programming reuses plans for relation subsets. Pass 1 chooses base-table access plans. Pass 2 combines pairs; later passes extend a retained subset plan by joining a relation not yet included.

For a candidate extension, estimate the complete accumulated cost: the retained subplan, access to the added relation and the chosen join operation, without double-counting reads already included in those components. Estimate result cardinality for later extensions.

The principle of optimality applies to states whose relevant output properties are represented. Retaining only one subplan per subset can lose the best complete plan if a more expensive subplan provides useful ordering.

PDF pp. 13–19

sections.title: Interesting orders and final plan cost
sections.html:
An interesting order may reduce later sorting for a join, GROUP BY, DISTINCT or ORDER BY. The optimiser retains the cheapest unordered plan plus the cheapest plan for each useful output order for a relation subset.

The Sailors/Reserves/Boats example retains alternatives ordered by sid or bid when those orders can benefit later operations. Plans are compared within the same required-property state rather than discarding every plan that is not immediately cheapest.

After all joins, add remaining grouping, aggregation, duplicate elimination and sorting costs. The selected plan is the cheapest within the searched space under the estimated statistics and cost model.

PDF pp. 20–24

quiz.question: Why retain a more expensive subplan that already produces sorted output?
options: Because sorted output is always better
Because it may avoid an expensive sort later
Because subplan cost does not matter
quiz.explanation: An interesting order can reduce the total plan cost by avoiding a later sort, even if that subplan costs more.

source.summary: The complete official PDF was read. Topics covered: Single-table access enumeration and cost; Join-tree combinatorial growth; Left-deep versus bushy/right-deep; Cross-product pruning; Dynamic programming and optimal substructure; Interesting orders and property-aware retention; Final grouping/sorting cost. The explanations and calculations above are original teaching material, not reproductions of the slides.
